headline: Apple avoided semiconductor tariffs last year thanks to Intel chip deal, WSJ reports
summary: Apple reportedly bypassed significant semiconductor tariffs last year due to a deal with Intel to produce chips in the U.S. This strategic move helped mitigate rising import costs.
details: Apple reportedly bypassed significant semiconductor tariffs last year, a move attributed to a strategic deal with Intel. The agreement involved Intel producing chips for Apple within the United States.

This domestic production helped Apple circumvent import duties that would otherwise apply to chips manufactured overseas. The Wall Street Journal reported on this development, highlighting the financial benefits for Apple.

Looking ahead, Intel is expected to manufacture at least some upcoming Mac and iPhone chips for Apple in the U.S. This partnership could deepen as Apple diversifies its supply chain and navigates global trade policies.

headline_marked: [[AI agents follow rules nearly perfectly]] when mechanically enforced: 149/150 tasks showed zero violations
headline: AI agents follow rules nearly perfectly when mechanically enforced: 149/150 tasks showed zero violations
summary: A new experiment found that mechanical enforcement, not rule phrasing, is key to AI agent compliance, with 99.3% rule adherence when safeguards were active, contradicting earlier anecdotal evidence.
details: An experiment involving 150 standardized tasks on DeepSeek V4 Pro tested AI coding agents' adherence to rules. It revealed a striking 99.3% compliance rate, with 149 out of 150 tasks showing zero rule violations.

This high compliance was attributed to a "GateGuard" system that mechanically blocked unverified Edit/Write operations during the experiment. This mechanical enforcement proved stronger than any effect of rule format (syllogism vs. imperative).

A retrospective baseline confirmed the impact: before GateGuard was implemented, sessions had a 55.9% rule violation rate. After its integration, this rate plummeted to 0.7%, demonstrating mechanical enforcement as the dominant factor.

Despite identical compliance rates, the study noted differences in reasoning depth. Syllogism agents anchored their actions in causal chains, while imperative agents used checklist tags, especially in design tasks where GateGuard didn't intervene.

The findings suggest that rule format influences *how* agents understand the rules, not *whether* they comply, when mechanical enforcement is present. Future research will include GateGuard-OFF replication and independent human rating to further explore these dynamics.
